J3b: It's a bit like the process of getting married. At first, you visit your girlfriend or boyfriend when schedules align and each of you agrees. Over time as you get closer to marriage (which hopefully is not a fully unconscious process), you start making decisions together and considering sharing more and more resources. Once married, if you decide to divorce, you split up the resources, although that's also contentious depending on how long the marriage was for, whether one person feels tricked, etc,  and unfortunately often ends up in court.  Leaving a commune is the divorce half of it, where the shared resources have to get split up. When joining or forming a commune, we can hopefully be more conscious about the process and less romantic.
J4: Friends who come to visit don't get written terms, though. That's not how anything works, and at first they don't even know if they'll stick around for a day or a week. There are implied terms, like be respectful and be honest, and those shouldn't need to be in writing. If someone is offered something like an internship or a probationary period, that would require written terms. Or if it naturally evolves and they bring up wanting something like that, it could be done.
R14b: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become a situation where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. A group starts out inviting honesty and ends up treating privacy as resistance. But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a dynamic, living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain. In general, people can have their own private practices, of course. But if they start worshipping Satan, they get booted.
R16c: It should go without saying that nobody has to take medicine to have equal respect in the community. But medicine is an optional part of the overall therapy process, and if a member is avoiding the therapy process and becoming hard to deal with, they will naturally not belong at a certain point. If it gets to the point of being impossible to live with, they will be kicked out. But nearly always, people who don't fit in leave way before that.
R16d: They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it's up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence. It depends on so many factors that I can't decide any of this ahead of time. It's up to the people involved.
R18b: It can be tricky to spell everything out, though. Let's say a grandmother is demonizing the commune. Cutting off contact with her could make things way worse. When it's tricky and dangerous for everyone like that, I think the commune needs to step in and help people decide how to communicate with outsiders. Nobody can give that advice ahead of time, including me. It has to be worked out in the moment, context by context.
